## Company: Monde Nissin Corporation (MONDE)
Sector: Industrial / Food, Beverage & Tobacco
Monde Nissin Corporation (MONDE) was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission on May 23, 1979 primarily to engage in manufacturing, processing, and baking, among others, all kinds of goods like candies, confectionaries, biscuits, cakes and other foods, drugs, and cosmetics.

MONDE has two core businesses namely, the Asia-Pacific branded food and beverage (F&B) business and the meat alternative business. The Asia-Pacific branded F&B business is further divided into the product groups of instant noodles, biscuits, and other products such as beverages, baked goods and culinary aid. Some of the brands under this business include "Lucky Me!", "SkyFlakes", "Fita", "Mama Sita's", and "Dutch Mill". The meat alternative business meanwhile has the "Quorn" and "Cauldron" brands.

The Company's wholly-owned subsidiaries are Monde Nissin Singapore Pte. Ltd. (MNSPL), Monde M.Y. San Corporation, and Monde Nissin International Investments Ltd. MNSPL wholly owns Monde Nissin (UK) Limited, which controls 100% of Marlow Foods Limited that manufactures the meat alternative products. MNSPL also owns 100% of Monde Nissin New Zealand Ltd. and 56.48% of Monde Nissin Thailand Co. Ltd.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

thesis:
Enough data. Writing thesis now.

---

Monde Nissin runs two distinct businesses that must be evaluated separately. The Asia-Pacific F&B operation — Lucky Me! instant noodles, SkyFlakes, Fita, Mama Sita's condiments, Dutch Mill beverages — is immediately understandable: mass-market everyday foods in a price-sensitive Philippine market where brand recognition and shelf presence compound over decades. This is a textbook consumer staples business with genuine meaning. Quorn, the UK-based mycoprotein meat alternative brand acquired in 2016, is a different animal — dependent on the alt-protein secular trend in Western markets that has turned out to be far more faddish and margin-thin than investors expected. The conglomerate structure makes MONDE harder to value cleanly.

The moat in the F&B segment is real and durable. Lucky Me! commands dominant share in the Philippine instant noodle market, competing directly against Nissin and Payless with the advantages of scale, deep distribution into sari-sari stores, and a decade of brand equity with Filipino households. SkyFlakes and Fita occupy similarly entrenched positions in the biscuit category — these aren't just products consumers prefer, they're products consumers reach for without thinking. Switching costs are low but habit formation and retail footprint create structural stickiness. The ROIC of 31.4% over ten years reflects a real cost advantage and pricing power in these categories. Quorn's moat is narrower: proprietary mycoprotein technology gives it a unique ingredient, but the broader alt-meat category is commoditizing and its UK-heavy revenue base left it exposed when consumer enthusiasm for plant-based eating cooled sharply post-2022.

Management has been navigating the Quorn drag reasonably well. Losses in the meat alternatives segment peaked at ₱966M in 2023, narrowed to ₱804M in 2024, fell again to ₱304M in 2025, and the division posted a core net income of ₱106M in the first half of 2026 — a genuine inflection. The restructuring appears to be working: Quorn expanded gross margins by 500+ basis points year-on-year in 2025, and core EBITDA turned positive. On the F&B side, Q1 2026 delivered 9.1% revenue growth. The 4.5% dividend yield and consistent cash returns signal management's willingness to return capital even while absorbing Quorn losses. No fraud signals. The Quorn acquisition itself remains a costly capital allocation mistake — they paid a premium for a trend that reversed — but they've been transparent about it and appear to be managing the exit toward profitability rather than doubling down.

Valuation is the hard stop. At ₱6.91, MONDE trades at 14.4x earnings with EPS growth of only 3.3% and a PEG of 4.39x — roughly four times what a Rule #1 investor would accept for this growth rate. The Rule #1 sticker price of ₱1.07 reflects a brutal truth: at 3.3% EPS growth, the earnings compounding over ten years simply does not justify today's price at any reasonable discount rate. Book value has declined over the period at -2.6% annually, and while FCF growth has been strong (115.3% ten-year average), much of that appears to be catch-up after Quorn's loss years rather than structural acceleration. The dividend yield of 4.5% is attractive in absolute terms but doesn't compensate for a price that's over 1,000% above the margin-of-safety buy price. To be fair, ₱1.07 feels mathematically aggressive — but even at twice or three times that estimate, MONDE at ₱6.91 is a hard sell on a Rule #1 framework.

Bottom line: pass at the current price. The Philippine F&B business is genuinely good — durable brands, real moat, competent management — and Quorn's turnaround is ahead of schedule, which could re-rate the stock if the division sustains profitability through 2026-2027. But paying 14x earnings for a company growing EPS at 3.3% leaves no margin of safety and no room for error. Watch for Quorn achieving full-year profitability and F&B EPS growth reaccelerating above 8-10%; if both happen and the price pulls back to the ₱5 range, the risk/reward conversation changes materially.
